passages.happening:
“Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (verse 1).

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
‘Therefore’ is a hinge. For eleven chapters Paul has told what God has done: mercy for Jew and Gentile, a right standing given freely, the Spirit, a love nothing can break. Now he turns to how believers should live. The order matters. The life comes after the mercy, and because of it. Paul does not say ‘live this way so that God will be merciful’. He says ‘God has been merciful, so live this way’.

Every hearer in Rome knew what a sacrifice was. Temples stood all over the city, and animals were killed on their altars every day. The Jews in Rome knew of the sacrifices at the temple in Jerusalem. A sacrifice was something given wholly to God, and usually it died.

Paul's picture is startling: a ‘living’ sacrifice. Not a dead animal on an altar, but a whole person, body included, given to God and still alive. Worship is no longer only what happens at an altar. It is what a person does with his body on an ordinary day.

‘This world’ means this present age, the way of life that runs without God. ‘Conformed’ means pressed into its shape, like clay in a mould. ‘Transformed’ means changed from the inside, the same word used of Jesus being changed in form before his disciples. The change begins in the mind, in how a person thinks.
passages.ot:
The idea that God wants the whole person, not only an offering, runs through Israel's Scriptures. David prays, “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17). Hosea says, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). A psalm says, “Sacrifice a thank offering to God” (Psalm 50:14), meaning a life of thanks.

The law of Moses required that an animal for sacrifice be without defect, wholly given. Paul uses the language of the altar for a whole life given to God.

‘Mercy’ in verse 1 ties this chapter to the end of chapter 11, where God has mercy on everyone (11:32). Everything Paul asks now flows from that mercy.
passages.hard:
Does ‘do not be conformed to this world’ mean that Christians should withdraw from society, or that everything outside the church is bad? Paul does not say so. The same letter tells believers to live at peace with everyone (verse 18), to respect rulers (13:1-7), and to do what is right ‘in the eyes of everybody’ (verse 17). Paul worked at a trade and lived in cities.

‘This world’ means the pattern of life that ignores God, not the created world or its people. Christians in different traditions draw the line between faithful difference and needless withdrawal in different places. The verse does not settle each case. What it asks is a mind being renewed, able to ‘test and approve’ God's will, not a list of things to avoid.
passages.asks: Think of your body as Paul does: something you can give to God today. Name one ordinary thing you will do with your hands, your eyes or your words this week, and offer it to him as worship.

passages.happening:
“For by the grace given me I say to every one of you: Do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but think of yourself with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith God has given you” (verse 3).

The body has many members, and they do different work (verse 4). Paul says, “so in Christ we who are many are one body, and each member belongs to one another” (verse 5).

“We have different gifts according to the grace given us” (verse 6). Paul names some: prophecy, serving, teaching, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy. Each should use his gift in its own way: the giver generously, the leader with diligence, the one who shows mercy cheerfully (verses 6-8).
passages.hearers:
Paul begins with humility. Before he speaks of gifts, he tells each person not to think too highly of himself. ‘Sober judgment’ means seeing yourself clearly, neither puffed up nor crushed.

Paul uses the body as a picture of the church, as he does in 1 Corinthians 12. A body needs every part, and no part is the whole. In Christ every member belongs to every other, and every part matters.

The house churches in Rome were mixed: Jew and Gentile, slave and free, women and men. In such a church it would be easy for some to think themselves more important. Paul says each person's gift comes from grace, so no one can boast of it.

Look at the list. Some gifts sound grand, like prophecy and leading. Others are quiet: serving, giving, showing mercy. Paul puts them side by side. The one who visits the sick ‘cheerfully’ is using a gift as truly as the one who teaches.

‘Prophecy’ here means speaking a word from God to build up the church. Paul says it should be used ‘in proportion to his faith’, and readers differ on whether that means the prophet's own faith or the church's shared faith.
passages.ot:
Humility before God is a theme of the wisdom books. Proverbs says, “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:7). Paul echoes it again in verse 16.

The Old Testament also shows God giving different gifts to different people for the good of his people. When the tabernacle was built, God filled craftsmen with skill for their work (Exodus 31:2-6). Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised that God would pour out his Spirit on all people (Joel 2:28), a promise Peter said was fulfilled at Pentecost.
passages.hard:
Do all these gifts continue today, especially prophecy? Christians differ, and these notes do not choose.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians, and other continuationists, hold that all the gifts named in the New Testament continue in the church today, prophecy among them. Cessationists hold that some gifts, such as prophecy in the sense of new revelation from God, belonged to the time of the apostles and then ceased. Many in between hold that prophecy continues as a gift of speaking God's truth to a situation, always tested by Scripture. The note on Acts 2:1-4 sets out these views more fully.

What all agree on is Paul's point here: every believer has a gift from grace, no gift is a reason for pride, and the gifts are for one another.
passages.asks: Paul's list includes quiet gifts: serving, giving, encouraging, showing mercy. Ask which of these comes naturally to you. Then ask whom you could serve with it this week, and do it cheerfully.

passages.happening:
“Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good” (verse 9).

“Be devoted to one another in brotherly love. Outdo yourselves in honoring one another” (verse 10). Do not let your zeal fade; keep your spirit on fire, serving the Lord (verse 11). “Be joyful in hope, patient in affliction, persistent in prayer” (verse 12).

“Share with the saints who are in need. Practice hospitality” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘Sincere’ translates a Greek word that means unfeigned, not pretended. It is built from the word for an actor on a stage. Paul wants love that is not acting a part: what you show is what is really there.

‘Brotherly love’ is the love of a family. The church was to be a family. ‘Outdo yourselves in honoring one another’ turned the world's way upside down. In Roman society people competed for honour. Paul tells believers to compete in giving honour away.

‘The saints’ means God's people, all believers, not only the famous few. Some in Rome were poor. Some were slaves. Some were travellers far from home. ‘Practice hospitality’ means opening your home to strangers, including believers passing through. Travelling believers often stayed in the homes of other believers, as Paul himself was staying with Gaius when he wrote (16:23). Phoebe, who very likely carried this letter, would soon need such a welcome in Rome (16:1-2).

Notice how practical this is. Love here is not a feeling. It is sharing food and money, opening the door, keeping on in prayer.
passages.ot:
‘Detest what is evil; cling to what is good’ echoes the prophet Amos: “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate” (Amos 5:15).

Hospitality has deep roots in Israel's story. Abraham ran to welcome three strangers at his tent and fed them (Genesis 18:1-8). The law told Israel, “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

Sharing with those in need is also a command of the law: “you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother” (Deuteronomy 15:7).
passages.asks: Love that is not acting a part. Ask where your kindness to someone is mostly for show. Then do one thing this week from Paul's list that no one will notice: share something with someone in need, or open your home.

passages.happening:
“Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse” (verse 14). “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (verse 15). Live in harmony. Do not be proud, but enjoy the company of the lowly (verse 16).

“Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (verse 17). “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (verse 18).

“Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord’” (verse 19). Instead, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head” (verse 20).

“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
‘Bless those who persecute you’ sounds like the words of Jesus: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Paul's hearers may have known the saying. They would need it. A few years after this letter, Christians in Rome were killed by Nero.

‘Enjoy the company of the lowly’ was hard in a city that ranked everyone. To eat with slaves and the poor as equals was strange. Paul asks for it.

‘If it is possible on your part.’ Paul is realistic. Peace takes two. A believer cannot always make peace, but he must not be the one who refuses it.

‘Leave room for God's wrath’ does not mean ‘evil does not matter’. It means the opposite: evil matters so much that God himself will judge it. Because God will do justice, believers do not have to take revenge. That frees them to do good even to an enemy.

‘Burning coals’ is a picture from Proverbs. What it means is debated; see the note below.
passages.ot:
Verse 19 quotes the Song of Moses: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35). The law had already said, “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

Verse 20 quotes Proverbs: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink” (Proverbs 25:21). The proverb goes on, “For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you” (Proverbs 25:22). Paul follows the Greek wording.

Some psalms ask God to take vengeance on enemies. The Psalms book page, in its part on the cursing psalms, reads many of them as honest prayer that hands vengeance to God instead of taking it, and quotes this very verse: Paul writes, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard:
What does it mean to ‘heap burning coals’ on an enemy's head? Readers differ. The reading many hold takes the coals as a picture of the burning shame that undeserved kindness can stir, which may lead an enemy to regret and to make peace. Others take the coals as a sign of judgment: if the enemy stays hostile after kindness, his guilt before God only grows. Some scholars have linked the picture to an Egyptian rite in which a person carried a dish of burning coals on his head as a sign of repentance, but the evidence for that link is thin and comes from a later time. The next verse helps: ‘overcome evil with good’ suggests Paul wants the enemy's good, not his ruin.

Does ‘overcome evil with good’ mean a person must stay where someone is hurting them? No. Blessing an enemy and leaving vengeance to God does not mean staying in danger or keeping silent about harm. Paul's call is not to let evil win. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Think of someone who has wronged you. Do not pretend it did not happen. Hand the judging of it to God in prayer, by name. Then ask what one good thing, safe and wise, you could do for that person, and pray for them.
